english: to grill / to roast / to bake
usage: The default verb at Korean BBQ — at a 고깃집 you 고기를 구워 먹어요 (grill it on the table and eat it yourself).
Same verb covers oven-baking: 빵을 굽다, 쿠키를 굽다, 케이크를 굽다. Korean doesn't split 'bake' from 'grill'.
노릇노릇하게 is the set onomatopoeic result-adverb for a nice browned surface — pairs almost only with 굽다/튀기다.
to grill over a wire rack
Names the tool: 석쇠 (grill rack), 숯불에 굽다 (over charcoal). 직화로 굽다 = grill over an open flame.
examples: 빵 구워요.
I'm baking bread.
Simplest possible frame — note the form is 구워요, never 굽어요; the dictionary ㅂ is already gone.
고기 다 구웠어요?
Is the meat all grilled?
The constant question at the table. 구웠어요 is the ㅂ-irregular past — it is NOT 굽었어요.
삼겹살은 제가 구울게요, 앉아 계세요.
I'll grill the pork belly, you stay seated.
구울게요 (ㅂ→우 + ㄹ게요) volunteers you for grill duty; said warmly to elders so they don't work.
nuance: 굽다 is a ㅂ-irregular verb: the dictionary ㅂ becomes 우 before any vowel ending, so the 요-form is 구워요 (not the textbook-looking 굽어요), past 구웠어요, future 구울 거예요 — memorize the 요-form and the rest follows. Meaning-wise it is dry-heat cooking with direct radiant heat: grilling meat, roasting, AND oven-baking bread all fall under this one word, which surprises English speakers who keep three separate verbs. Contrast it sharply with its kitchen neighbours: 굽다 uses no water and little-to-no oil (just the surface), whereas 볶다 tosses food in a little oil and 튀기다 submerges it in lots of oil. It is the single most useful cooking verb for a foreigner here because 구이 (grilled dishes) and Korean BBQ are everywhere. The classic learner trap is writing 굽어요/굽었어요 by analogy with regular verbs — say 구워요/구웠어요.

mistakes: Conjugating it as a regular verb: 굽어요/굽었어요. It's ㅂ-irregular, so the ㅂ→우 gives 구워요/구웠어요.
Using 굽다 for boiling or deep-frying. Boiling a solid is 삶다, boiling a liquid is 끓이다, and deep-frying is 튀기다 — 굽다 is dry direct heat only.
Forgetting the ㅂ drops before consonant endings too in the future/modifier: it's 구울 거예요 and 구운 고기, not 굽을 거예요/굽은 고기.

english: to stir-fry / to pan-fry (with little oil)
usage: Stir-frying aged kimchi is a home staple (김치볶음밥, 볶음김치) — 볶다 implies tossing in a hot pan with a little oil.
Use 볶다 for quick high-heat tossing; the noun 볶음 then names dishes — 제육볶음, 오징어볶음, 낙지볶음.
센 불 (strong flame) is the set partner: 볶다 is fast and hot, so 센 불에 빨리 볶다 is the natural phrasing.
to coat the pan with oil and stir-fry
기름을 두르다 (drizzle/coat oil) is the step that always precedes 볶다 — a little oil, not a deep pool.
examples: 채소 볶아요.
I'm stir-frying vegetables.
Bare-bones frame; 볶아요 keeps the bright ㅏ vowel because the stem vowel ㅗ is bright — never 볶어요.
밥이랑 김치 넣고 같이 볶았어요.
I put in the rice and kimchi and stir-fried them together.
The 김치볶음밥 move; 같이 볶다 = toss everything together. Past 볶았어요.
기름 두르고 마늘부터 볶을까요?
Shall we coat the pan with oil and stir-fry the garlic first?
볶을까요? proposes a cooking step to whoever is cooking with you; …부터 = 'starting with'.
nuance: 볶다 is a regular verb and, because its stem vowel ㅗ is 'bright', it takes 아 endings: 볶아요, 볶았어요, never 볶어요. It means stir-frying or pan-frying in a SMALL amount of oil over high heat while constantly moving the food, so picture a wok-style toss. The dividing lines learners blur: 볶다 = a little oil + tossing; 튀기다 = a deep pool of oil + submerging (deep-fry); 부치다 = a thin film of oil for flat foods like 전/jeon; 굽다 = dry direct heat, no real oil. Tons of restaurant dish names freeze the noun form 볶음 onto the end (제육볶음 stir-fried pork, 낙지볶음 stir-fried octopus), so recognizing this verb lets you decode menus. The English pitfall is mapping every 'fry' to one word — English 'fry' splits in Korean into 볶다/튀기다/부치다, and choosing wrong changes the whole dish.

mistakes: Translating English 'fry' as 볶다 when you mean deep-fry. Deep-frying in lots of oil is 튀기다; 볶다 is only a little oil with tossing.
Using 볶다 for pancake-style flat foods. Pan-frying 전/jeon or 부침개 is 부치다 (전을 부치다), not 볶다.
Writing 볶어요. The stem vowel is bright (ㅗ), so the ending is 아 → 볶아요/볶았어요.

usage: 삶다 = cooking a SOLID food submerged in boiling water (eggs, noodles, potatoes), versus 끓이다 (boil a liquid / make soup).
For pasta, 국수, or 칼국수 you 면을 삶아요. The word is pronounced [삼따] — the ㄹ of the ㄻ batchim is silent here.
푹 (thoroughly, until soft) is the signature partner adverb: 푹 삶다 = simmer-boil until fork-tender.
The past-attributive 삶은 + noun labels the result: 삶은 계란, 삶은 감자, 삶은 면 — how menus and recipes name them.
examples: 계란 삶아요.
I'm boiling eggs.
Simplest frame; 삶아요 keeps the bright ㅏ vowel — it is NOT 삶어요.
감자를 푹 삶았어요.
I boiled the potatoes until soft.
푹 삶다 = boil thoroughly until tender, a very natural collocation. Past 삶았어요.
국수 삶을게요, 양념장 좀 만들어 주세요.
I'll boil the noodles, please make the sauce.
삶을게요 splits the kitchen tasks; …을게요 commits you to the noodle job.
nuance: 삶다 means to cook a solid food by fully submerging it in boiling water — eggs, noodles, potatoes, greens, even towels for sanitizing. The stem vowel ㅏ is bright, so endings take 아: 삶아요, 삶았어요 (never 삶어요), and the ㄻ batchim is pronounced [삼], giving [삼따]/[살마]. The crucial, constantly-confused boundary is 삶다 vs 끓이다: 삶다 = put a solid INTO water to cook the solid (계란을 삶다); 끓이다 = boil the LIQUID itself or make a brothy dish (물을 끓이다, 찌개를 끓이다). English 'boil' covers both, which is exactly why learners misfire — they say 계란을 끓이다 (literally 'bring the egg to a boil') when they mean 계란을 삶다. Compare also 데치다, which is only a quick few-second blanch, whereas 삶다 is full cooking-through.

mistakes: Saying 계란을 끓이다 for 'boil an egg'. Boiling a solid IN water is 삶다 → 계란을 삶다; 끓이다 is for boiling a liquid or making soup.
Writing 삶어요. The stem vowel is bright (ㅏ), so the ending is 아 → 삶아요/삶았어요.
Confusing it with 데치다. 삶다 cooks food fully through; 데치다 is only a brief blanch of a few seconds.

usage: 찐만두 (steamed mandu) vs 군만두 (pan-fried) — the verb on the menu tells you the cooking method.
찐 고구마 is a beloved winter snack. 찌다 = cook with steam, which keeps the food moist.
Names the tool: 찜기 (steamer basket). Related is the dish-type 찜 (갈비찜, 아구찜) cooked by steaming/braising.
The past-attributive 찐 + noun marks steamed foods: 찐빵, 찐 옥수수, 찐 감자 — recognizable street-snack vocabulary.
examples: 만두 쪄요.
I'm steaming dumplings.
Bare frame showing the contraction: 찌 + 어 → 쪄, never the spelled-out 찌어요.
호박을 살짝 쪘어요.
I lightly steamed the zucchini.
쪘어요 is the past (찌 + 었 → 쪘); 살짝 (lightly/briefly) pairs naturally with gentle steaming.
우리 같이 떡 찔까요?
Shall we steam rice cakes together?
찔까요? proposes steaming as the method; the stem is just 찌-, so the future modifier is 찔 (not 찌을).
nuance: 찌다 is a single-syllable ㅣ-stem verb, so ㅣ + 어 contracts to ㅕ: the 요-form is 쪄요 and the past is 쪘어요 — a spot where beginners wrongly write 찌어요/찌었어요. It means cooking with steam (hot vapor rising through 찜기), which keeps food moist and soft, and you'll meet it as the 찐- prefix on snacks (찐만두, 찐빵, 찐 고구마) and in the related dish-name suffix 찜 (갈비찜). Distinguish it from its wet-heat neighbours: 삶다 submerges the food in water, 끓이다 boils a liquid, but 찌다 keeps the food ABOVE the water in vapor. The sharpest pitfall, though, is the homonym: this 찌다 is spelled and conjugated identically to the 찌다 in 살이 찌다 ('to gain weight'), so 쪘어요 could mean 'I steamed it' or 'I gained weight' — only context and an object (만두를 쪘어요 vs 살이 쪘어요) tell them apart.

usage: 튀기다 = cook fully submerged in hot oil. The noun 튀김 then names dishes — 새우튀김, 야채튀김, 오징어튀김.
Always implies a deep pool of oil at high heat, unlike 볶다 (stir-fry with just a little oil).
바삭하게 (crisp/crunchy) is the signature result-adverb for 튀기다 — the whole point of deep-frying.
튀김옷 (literally 'frying clothes' = batter/breading) is what you 입히다 (dress on) before you 튀기다.
examples: 새우 튀겨요.
I'm deep-frying shrimp.
Simplest frame; the contracted form is 튀겨요, never the spelled-out 튀기어요.
새우를 바삭하게 튀겼어요.
I deep-fried the shrimp until crispy.
바삭하게 = until crispy, the classic result phrase for 튀기다; past 튀겼어요.
기름 뜨거우니까 튀길 때 조심하세요.
The oil is hot, so be careful when deep-frying.
튀길 때 = 'when deep-frying'; a natural safety reminder. …으니까 gives the reason.
nuance: 튀기다 is a regular ㅣ-stem verb where ㅣ + 어 contracts to ㅕ, so it is 튀겨요/튀겼어요, not 튀기어요/튀기었어요. It specifically means cooking food fully submerged in plenty of hot oil — deep-frying — and the noun form 튀김 plasters menus and 분식 stalls (새우튀김, 오징어튀김, 모둠튀김), so the verb is worth learning just to order. The lines English speakers smear together: 튀기다 = a deep pool of oil, food submerged; 볶다 = a little oil, food tossed (stir-fry); 부치다 = a thin film of oil for flat foods (전/jeon); 굽다 = dry heat, essentially no oil. Because English 'fry' alone is ambiguous, learners over-use 튀기다 for anything cooked in a pan when they often mean 볶다 or 부치다. One more note: 튀기다 also means 'to bounce/flick' (공을 튀기다), but in daily food talk the deep-fry sense dominates.

Writing 튀기어요/튀기었어요. The ㅣ-stem contracts: 튀기 + 어 → 튀겨요, past 튀겼어요.
Forgetting the future/modifier drops the 이: it's 튀길 거예요 and 튀긴 새우, not 튀기을 거예요/튀기은 새우.

english: to boil (a liquid) / to make (soup, stew, ramyeon)
usage: The fixed phrase for cooking instant ramyeon. Koreans never say 라면을 만들다 for cooking it — it's always 끓이다.
끓이다 = bring a liquid to a boil or simmer a brothy dish: 찌개를 끓이다, 국을 끓이다, 죽을 끓이다.
to boil hard / at a rolling boil
팔팔 is the onomatopoeic adverb for a vigorous rolling boil — 팔팔 끓이다 / 물이 팔팔 끓다.
Any brothy 국/찌개/탕 is 끓이다, not 만들다 — the act of simmering IS the cooking, so the verb means 'make' here.
examples: 라면 끓여요.
I'm making ramyeon.
Bare everyday frame; the contracted form is 끓여요, never 끓이어요.
된장찌개를 끓였어요.
I made soybean-paste stew.
끓이다 is THE verb for making any 찌개/국 — 만들다 sounds wrong here. Past 끓였어요.
제가 라면 끓여 줄까요?
Shall I make you some ramyeon?
끓여 줄까요? offers to cook for someone — an extremely common, friendly line. …아/어 주다 = do it for you.
nuance: 끓이다 is the causative/transitive partner of 끓다 ('to be boiling'): you 끓이다 a liquid so that it 끓다. As a ㅣ-stem it contracts ㅣ + 어 → ㅕ, giving 끓여요/끓였어요 (not 끓이어요). Use it for boiling water and, crucially, for MAKING any brothy dish — 찌개, 국, 탕, 죽, and famously 라면 (라면을 끓이다 is frozen usage; never 라면을 만들다). The boundary learners must nail is 끓이다 vs 삶다: 끓이다 acts on the LIQUID or the dish (물을 끓이다, 김치찌개를 끓이다), while 삶다 acts on a SOLID dropped into water (계란을 삶다, 면을 삶다). English 'boil' flattens this distinction, so beginners say 라면을 삶다 or 계란을 끓이다 and sound off. Picture it this way: if the water is the point, 끓이다; if a solid going INTO the water is the point, 삶다.

Writing 끓이어요/끓이었어요. The ㅣ-stem contracts: 끓이 + 어 → 끓여요, past 끓였어요.

usage: Step one of most 나물 side dishes: a quick dunk in boiling water, then drain and season (무치다).
데치다 already means a SHORT dunk, so 살짝 데치다 ('blanch lightly') is almost redundant — yet extremely common and natural.
끓는 물에 (in boiling water) is the standard prepositional partner — the water must already be at a boil.
데치다 + 무치다 is the frozen two-step recipe of Korean banchan: blanch the green, then dress it.
examples: 콩나물 데쳐요.
I'm blanching bean sprouts.
Simplest frame; the contraction is 데쳐요 (데치 + 어 → 데쳐), never 데치어요.
시금치를 살짝 데쳤어요.
I quickly blanched the spinach.
데쳤어요 is the past; 살짝 (just briefly) is the signature partner for a short blanch.
나물 같이 데칠까요?
Shall I blanch the greens with you?
데칠까요? offers to do the blanching step; the stem drops 이 in the modifier → 데칠 (not 데치을).
nuance: 데치다 is a regular ㅣ-stem verb (데쳐요/데쳤어요, ㅣ + 어 → ㅕ) meaning a quick blanch: dropping vegetables (or sometimes squid, bean sprouts) into already-boiling water for just a handful of seconds to soften them and set their color, then immediately draining. It is a PREP step, not full cooking, which is the line that separates it from 삶다 (boil a solid all the way through) and 끓이다 (boil a liquid / simmer a dish). It is the gateway move of Korean 나물 banchan: 데치다 then 무치다 (season). The pitfall that trips English speakers is the near-twin 데우다 ('to reheat/warm up already-cooked food'): same friendly 데- start, totally different job — 국을 데우다 reheats yesterday's soup, while 시금치를 데치다 blanches raw spinach. Mixing them up makes a recipe nonsensical, so anchor 데치다 = raw → boiling water → quick dunk.

데치다 is a regular ㅣ-stem verb (ㅣ + 어 → ㅕ): 데쳐요, 데쳤어요, and the stem drops 이 in the modifier → 데칠.

The pitfall that trips English speakers is the near-twin 데우다 ('to reheat/warm up already-cooked food'): same friendly 데- start, totally different job — 국을 데우다 reheats yesterday's soup, while 시금치를 데치다 blanches raw spinach. Anchor 데치다 = raw → boiling water → quick dunk.

mistakes: Confusing 데치다 with 데우다. 데치다 = blanch raw food in boiling water; 데우다 = reheat already-cooked food (국을 데우다).
Treating 데치다 as full boiling. It's only a brief few-second dunk; cooking a solid all the way through is 삶다.
Writing 데치어요/데치었어요. The ㅣ-stem contracts: 데치 + 어 → 데쳐요, past 데쳤어요.

english: to season and toss (by hand) / to dress (a salad/namul)
usage: The defining verb of Korean side dishes: mix blanched greens with 양념 by hand. The noun 무침 names dishes — 오이무침, 골뱅이무침.
무치다 means coating an ingredient evenly with seasoning/sauce, usually by hand or with tongs.
조물조물 is the onomatopoeic adverb for gently squeezing seasoning in by hand — almost exclusively paired with 무치다.
Taste-adverbs in -하게 are the natural partners: 새콤하게 (tangy), 매콤하게 (spicy), 짭짤하게 (savory-salty) 무치다.
examples: 시금치 무쳐요.
I'm seasoning the spinach.
Bare frame; the contraction is 무쳐요 (무치 + 어 → 무쳐), never 무치어요.
시금치를 참기름에 무쳤어요.
I dressed the spinach with sesame oil.
참기름에 무치다 is the quintessential namul finish; past 무쳤어요.
콩나물 데쳐서 무칠까요?
Shall we blanch the bean sprouts and then season them?
데치다 + 무치다 = the standard banchan two-step; 무칠까요? proposes the dressing step.
nuance: 무치다 is the hands-on tossing that FINISHES most Korean banchan: you blanch (데치다) a vegetable, then 무치다 it with 양념 — sesame oil, garlic, soy or gochujang — until every strand is evenly coated, traditionally squeezing it 조물조물 by hand. As a ㅣ-stem it contracts to 무쳐요/무쳤어요. The noun 무침 labels a whole menu category of cold seasoned dishes (오이무침, 골뱅이무침, 무생채). The contrast learners MUST keep straight is 무치다 vs 비비다: 무치다 means DRESSING/coating a single ingredient with seasoning so it absorbs the flavor (a side dish), whereas 비비다 means STIRRING many components together into one mixed dish (비빔밥, 비빔국수). They feel similar in English ('mix/toss'), but a Korean would never say 밥을 무치다 for bibimbap or 나물을 비비다 for seasoned spinach. Anchor it: 무치다 = season one thing; 비비다 = stir everything together.

Using the wrong particle for the seasoning: it's 참기름에 무치다 (에 = with/in the seasoning), not 참기름을 무치다.

english: to slice / to cut (food, on a board)
usage: 썰다 is the kitchen-specific 'cut' — slicing food on a board (도마). Far more natural than 자르다 for prepping food.
Pairs with manner-adverbs: 얇게 (thinly), 두껍게 (thickly), 채 썰다 (julienne), 깍둑썰다 (dice into cubes).
송송 is the onomatopoeic adverb for chopping scallions into little rounds — 대파를 송송 썰다 is a set phrase.
어슷썰기 (diagonal slicing) is a standard recipe cut for 대파/고추 — 어슷하게 썰다 or just 어슷썰다.
examples: 양파 썰어요.
I'm slicing onions.
Bare frame; the ㄹ stays before the vowel ending → 썰어요, not 써요.
고기를 한입 크기로 썰었어요.
I cut the meat into bite-sized pieces.
썰었어요 keeps the ㄹ before 었; 한입 크기로 = into bite-size. …(으)로 marks the resulting shape.
제가 대파 썰까요?
Shall I slice the green onion?
썰까요? — the ㄹ DROPS before the ㄲ of 까, so it's 썰까 (not 썰을까).
nuance: 썰다 is a ㄹ-irregular (ㄹ-dropping) verb: the stem ㄹ vanishes before endings starting with ㄴ/ㅂ/ㅅ and before the ㄹ of -(으)ㄹ, giving 썹니다, 써세요, 썰 거예요, 썰까요? — but the ㄹ STAYS before vowel endings, so 썰어요/썰었어요. In the kitchen 썰다 is the natural verb for slicing food on a 도마 (cutting board), much more idiomatic than the general-purpose 자르다, which you'd use for cutting paper, hair, or a rope. The dividing line: 자르다 = cut/sever anything into pieces (broad); 썰다 = rhythmically slice food with a knife on a board (specific). Learn it bundled with the cutting adverbs you'll meet in every recipe — 얇게, 채 썰다 (julienne), 어슷하게, 송송, 깍둑썰다 — because Korean encodes the cut SHAPE in these adverbs rather than in the verb. The English-speaker trap is leaning on 자르다 for all cutting; for food prep, 썰다 is what sounds like a cook.

mistakes: Keeping the ㄹ before ㅂ/ㅅ endings. It drops: 썹니다 and 써세요, not 썰습니다/썰으세요.

Using 자르다 for everything in the kitchen. Slicing food on a board is more naturally 썰다; save 자르다 for paper, hair, rope.

usage: 다진 마늘 (minced garlic) goes into nearly every Korean recipe; you can even buy it pre-minced at the mart.
잘게 (into tiny pieces) is the natural partner adverb — finer than 썰다, almost to a paste.
The past-attributive 다진 + noun names pre-minced ingredients: 다진 고기, 다진 양파, 다진 생강.
곱게 (smoothly/finely) is used when you want an even, almost-paste texture — 마늘을 곱게 다지다.
examples: 마늘 다져요.
I'm mincing garlic.
Bare frame; the contraction is 다져요 (다지 + 어 → 다져), never 다지어요.
마늘이랑 양파를 잘게 다졌어요.
I finely minced the garlic and onion.
잘게 다지다 = mince finely; past 다졌어요. …이랑 = casual 'and'.
생강도 좀 다져 주세요.
Please mince some ginger too.
다져 주세요 asks for an ingredient to be minced; …도 = 'too/also'.
nuance: 다지다 means chopping something into very fine, near-uniform bits — distinctly finer than 썰다, often almost a paste. As a regular ㅣ-stem it contracts to 다져요/다졌어요. It shows up constantly as the past-attributive 다진 (다진 마늘, 다진 고기, 다진 파) on recipe cards and product labels, so it's worth recognizing even before you cook much — 다진 마늘 and ground meat (다진 고기) are pantry basics. The boundary with 썰다 is purely about FINENESS and motion: 썰다 is rhythmic slicing into visible pieces on a board, while 다지다 is repeated fine chopping until the pieces are tiny. Note the same verb has a vivid non-food sense, 'to firm up / consolidate' (기초를 다지다 'lay a firm foundation', 마음을 다지다 'steel one's resolve), but the kitchen meaning is what you'll use daily. English-speaker pitfall: don't reach for the present-participle 다지는 when you want the finished 'minced' — Korean uses the past-attributive 다진 for that already-minced state.

english: to mix together (by stirring) / to rub
usage: 비비다 is the verb hiding inside 비빔밥 — you 밥을 비벼 먹어요, stirring rice with toppings and gochujang.
Outside the kitchen, 비비다 means rubbing two surfaces together: 눈을 비비다, 손을 비비다, 등을 비비다.
골고루 (evenly, all over) is the natural partner — the goal of 비비다 is even distribution: 양념이 골고루 비벼지게.
The sauce takes 에: 고추장에/참기름에 비비다 = stir it together with gochujang/sesame oil.
examples: 밥 비벼요.
I'm mixing the rice.
Bare bibimbap frame; the contraction is 비벼요 (비비 + 어 → 비벼), never 비비어요.
고추장 넣고 잘 비벼서 드세요.
Add gochujang and mix it well before eating.
비벼서 드세요 = mix it, then eat — the standard table instruction. 잘 = well/thoroughly.
우리 비빔국수 같이 비빌까요?
Shall we mix the spicy noodles together?
비빌까요? proposes the mixing; note the near-pun of 비빔(국수) and the verb 비비다.
nuance: 비비다 means mixing by stirring and tossing many things together until evenly combined — it is literally the root of 비빔밥 and 비빔국수 (비빔 = the noun 'mixing'). As a regular ㅣ-stem it contracts to 비벼요/비볐어요. The contrast cooks must keep straight is 비비다 vs 무치다: 비비다 STIRS several components into one mixed dish (rice + toppings + sauce → bibimbap), whereas 무치다 DRESSES a single ingredient with seasoning so it soaks in (a side dish like 나물). English 'mix/toss' covers both, so beginners blur them — but 밥을 무치다 or 나물을 비비다 both sound wrong to a Korean. Beyond food, the same verb means physically rubbing two surfaces (눈을 비비다 'rub your eyes', 손을 비비다 'rub your hands', often in a pleading gesture), which is a handy everyday extension. Anchor it: at the table, 비비다 = stir it all together and eat.

english: to cool (something) down / to let cool
usage: 식히다 is the causative of 식다 ('to cool off'): you 식히다 hot food so it 식다. Handy before serving kids or eating.
to let it cool, then eat
식혀서 먹다 / 식혀서 드세요 is an everyday caretaking phrase you'll both hear and say at the table.
to let the steam/heat off briefly
한 김 식히다 (let one 'breath' of steam escape) = let it cool just a moment — a very natural set phrase.
to cool it because it's hot
뜨겁다 → 뜨거우니까 식히다 is the habitual pairing: the reason (too hot) plus the action (cool it).
examples: 국 좀 식혀요.
Cool the soup down a bit.
Bare frame; the contraction is 식혀요 (식히 + 어 → 식혀), never 식히어요. 좀 softens it to a request.
빵을 한 김 식혔어요.
I let the bread cool for a moment.
한 김 식히다 = let the heat off briefly; past 식혔어요.
커피 너무 뜨거우니까 좀 식혀서 드세요.
The coffee's too hot, so let it cool a bit before drinking.
식혀서 드세요 tells someone to let it cool first — caring and natural; …으니까 gives the reason.
nuance: 식히다 is the causative/transitive partner of intransitive 식다: 식다 means food cools off BY ITSELF (국이 식다 'the soup goes cold'), while 식히다 means YOU actively cool it — blowing on it, fanning it, leaving it out. The -히- is the causative infix, and as a ㅣ-stem it contracts to 식혀요/식혔어요. The key grammatical pitfall is transitivity: 식히다 takes an object (국을 식히다), whereas 식다 cannot, so '국을 식다' is ungrammatical — if there's a thing being cooled, you need 식히다. It's genuinely warm, useful table language: telling someone 식혀서 드세요 ('let it cool before eating') shows care. The other trap is the sound-alike 시키다, which means 'to order (food)' or 'to make someone do something' (숙제를 시키다); 식히다 and 시키다 are pronounced very similarly but are unrelated — 음식을 식히다 cools the food, 음식을 시키다 orders the food.
